A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same persona-augmented benchmarking study. Text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching v1 Appendix H to v2 Appendix I.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of ten LLMs on persona-rephrased CoQA, CosmosQA and DS-1000, alongside linguistic, filtering and ranking analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds experiments measuring sensitivity to disagreement between entailment checkers.

M1.justification: Persona selection, rephrasing, entailment filtering and post-stratified scoring remain unchanged. Both entailment models already appeared in v1. The added disagreement analysis evaluates uncertainty in the existing pipeline rather than establishing a revised augmentation algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions use CoQA, CosmosQA and DS-1000 with the same persona coverage, including the supplementary 500-base-persona experiment. The new analysis varies inclusion of existing disputed rephrasings without introducing another task, domain or population.

E2.justification: The original-prompt and Standard American English baselines, ten evaluated LLMs and entailment candidates in Table 5 are retained. Gemma-3-27b-it and Qwen-3-32b were already evaluated in v1; their new disagreement analysis introduces no new comparator.

E3.justification: New Appendix H introduces agreement-based evaluation sets supplemented with 25%, 50%, 75% or 100% of disputed examples. This adds a filtering-sensitivity protocol; the existing benchmark splits, metrics, model configurations and generation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix H adds a substantial robustness study addressing whether entailment-checker disagreement affects performance disparities and identification of poorly performing personas across all three benchmarks. v1 included checker-selection and filtering checks, but no corresponding disputed-example sensitivity analysis.

E5.justification: v2 introduces performance uncertainty ranges obtained from minimum and maximum outcomes across disagreement mixtures and ten reshuffles, displayed in Figure 7. This substantially extends uncertainty reporting beyond v1's existing diversity standard errors and statistical analyses. These are sensitivity ranges, not specified confidence intervals; the existing 25 repetitions for diversity estimation are retained.

E6.justification: New findings include worse results approximately 88% of the time when disputed examples are included, reported shifts of about four percentage points downward and two upward, and persistence of worst-performing personas. Figure 7 adds results under these filtering configurations. Existing numerical tables and matched plots retain their results.

T1.justification: Appendix D retains the same mathematical definitions and five equations for aggregation and post-stratification. Appendix H describes an empirical sensitivity procedure without adding a theorem, proof or formal guarantee.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: diversifying benchmarks through personas, demonstrating writing-style sensitivity and identifying consistently high- or low-performing styles. The added robustness evidence supports these existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the asymmetric uncertainty ranges and persistence of worst-performing personas as evidence that the findings withstand entailment-model disagreement. This adds a specific empirical rationale to the existing conservative-filtering argument. Limitations concerning synthetic personas and authentic human representation remain.

D1.justification: Appendix H adds instructions for constructing agreement/disagreement sets, resampling disputed examples and selecting minimum/maximum performance outcomes. Existing prompt templates, hardware, numerical precision, temperature and context-length disclosures in Appendices C and E are unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning relative to PersonaHub, demographic paraphrasing and writing-style evaluation are unchanged. Reference reflow and formatting do not introduce or remove prior work.

P1.justification: v2 expands the baseline explanation in Section 3.4, separates entailment and evaluation model descriptions, rewrites the diversity-results passage and ethical considerations, and inserts Appendix H before the retained experimental-results appendix. The overall narrative and section organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds the three-panel uncertainty Figure 7 and makes limited spacing, pagination and caption changes; existing figures and tables are retained. Revised captions for Figures 12 and 13 incorrectly identify the CosmosQA and DS-1000 correlation plots as CoQA, whereas the corresponding v1 captions identify them correctly.

improvement.justification: Appendix H and Figure 7 provide a useful quantitative check of filtering sensitivity that v1 lacked, while Section 3.4 explains the baselines more clearly. This improves evidential transparency without fully resolving entailment validity. The benefits outweigh localized reporting defects, including inconsistent 20th-percentile versus quartile descriptions and the incorrect dataset labels in Figures 12 and 13.
